draft.title: Life on reserves and stations
card: Reserves and stations were areas of land where many Aboriginal people in NSW were made to live, or felt they had to live. They were run by managers, and the rules came from outside the community.

Managers could control daily life. They could decide who lived on the land, where people worked, who could visit and what people could do. Women were also controlled, and many worked as domestic servants in colonists' homes.
Living conditions were often poor. Housing was crowded, rations were small and people had little say in decisions about their own lives.
Aboriginal people kept culture, family and resistance alive. They passed on stories and language, cared for their families and communities, and spoke out and acted against unfair rules.
draft.remember: Aboriginal people faced strict controls on reserves and stations, and still kept culture, family and resistance alive.

a.q: Which statement best describes life on reserves and stations for Aboriginal people?
opts: They faced controls but kept culture and family alive
They lived freely and managers had no say over them
They gave up their culture and stopped resisting
They were controlled, so their communities ended
a.why: Managers controlled many parts of daily life, but people kept stories, language and family ties going and also resisted. Saying that controls ended culture is tempting, but the card shows culture continued.
a.clue: Think about what was done to people and what they did in return.

b.q: On a reserve in NSW, a manager forbids a family from visiting relatives. The family still shares stories and language with their children at home. What does this show?
opts: Controls were real, yet culture and family continued
The manager's rules had no effect on the family
The family had accepted the manager's control fully
Culture could only survive if people left the reserve
b.why: The ban shows how managers controlled daily life, while the family's storytelling shows culture and family being kept alive. The option saying the rules had no effect is tempting, but the family was still limited by them.
b.clue: Look for both the control and the survival in the scenario.

a.best: They faced controls but kept culture and family alive

b.best: Controls were real, yet culture and family continued

problems.detail: The card says reserves and stations 'were run by managers'. In NSW, stations had resident managers, but many reserves had no manager and were overseen by local police. Saying all reserves were run by managers blurs a real distinction. Question b repeats this by placing a manager on a reserve.

check.summary: Both questions are sound and each has one clear right answer. The card wrongly says all reserves and stations were run by managers, when many NSW reserves had no manager and were supervised by police; the scenario in question b repeats this.

proposal.title: Life on reserves and stations
card: Reserves and stations were areas of land where many Aboriginal people in NSW were made to live, or felt they had to live. The rules came from outside the community.
Stations had a manager who lived on site. Many reserves had no manager and were watched over by local police instead.

Managers and police could control daily life: who lived there, who could visit, where people worked and when they could leave. Women's lives were also controlled, and many worked as domestic servants in colonists' homes. Housing was often crowded and rations were small.
Aboriginal people kept culture, family and resistance alive. They passed on stories and language, cared for their families and communities, and spoke out and acted against unfair rules.
proposal.remember: Aboriginal people faced controls on reserves and stations, and still kept culture, family and resistance alive.
